clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in SLC45A2 (also called MATP) and is a leading cause of oculocutaneous albinism in the Japanese population while occurring worldwide.
The phenotype is frequently indistinguishable from OCA2, with white-to-cream skin, white-to-yellow hair and the full range of ocular features, so subtype assignment depends on molecular testing.
Ocular hallmarks include congenital nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, iris transillumination, reduced acuity, photophobia and chiasmal misrouting.
Pigment may increase modestly with age in some individuals, as also seen in OCA2.
SLC45A2 encodes a melanosomal transporter that helps regulate melanosomal pH and tyrosinase processing.
Lifelong photoprotection and dermatological surveillance are required because of high ultraviolet susceptibility.
Visual impairment is usually stable; refractive correction and low-vision support are beneficial.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; genetic confirmation guides counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: OCA4 is caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC45A2 on chromosome 5, encoding a melanosomal solute-carrier (membrane-associated transporter) protein. This transporter contributes to regulation of melanosomal pH and thereby to the correct processing, sorting and activity of tyrosinase during melanogenesis. Impaired SLC45A2 function reduces melanin synthesis across skin, hair and the eye. The resulting phenotype overlaps closely with OCA2 because both mechanisms converge on melanosomal maturation, and reduced ocular melanin during development produces foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus and misrouting of optic-nerve fibres at the chiasm.
additionalDifferentials: Oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (OCA2) — often clinically identical, distinguished only by genetics.
Other OCA subtypes such as OCA6 (SLC24A5) and OCA7.
Syndromic albinism — Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes.
Griscelli and related pigmentary or immunological syndromes.
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment — acuity, nystagmus, iris transillumination and refraction.
Optical coherence tomography to document foveal hypoplasia.
Visual evoked potentials to detect chiasmal misrouting.
Molecular genetic testing including SLC45A2 within an oculocutaneous albinism panel.
Dermatological examination and cutaneous malignancy surveillance.
Screening for syndromic features to exclude Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes.
redFlags: New or changing skin lesions suggesting cutaneous malignancy.
A bleeding tendency raising suspicion of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome.
Recurrent infections or silvery hair suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Rapidly deteriorating vision, which is atypical and warrants review for an alternative diagnosis.
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is normal and the visual deficit, though permanent, is typically stable. Ultraviolet-related skin cancer is the main preventable risk and is reduced by consistent photoprotection and skin surveillance.
pitfalls: Attempting to distinguish OCA4 from OCA2 on appearance alone rather than by molecular testing.
Under-recognising OCA4 outside Japanese populations, where it is also present.
Omitting visual evoked potentials, so chiasmal misrouting is missed.
Neglecting screening for syndromic albinism with systemic implications.
